source_text: Unum ex his verum est, alterum falsum Verum est quod adulteriorum culpam homo, qui inde nascitur, non potest excusare, quia quod adulteri fecerunt, ad vitium pertinet voluntatis; quod autem genuerunt, ad laudem spectat fecunditatis, quia, si quis furtivum triticum serat, non nascitur messis obnoxia. Vitupero itaque furem, sed laudo segetem. Innocentem pronuntio qui nascitur ex generositate seminum, dicente Apostolo: Deus illi dat corpus prout vult, et unicuique seminum proprium corpus 79; condemno vero flagitiosum, qui ex propositi perversitate peccavit
pass_a_gloss: It is true that the human being who is born from there cannot excuse the guilt of adulteries, because what the adulterers did belongs to the vice of the will; but what they begot looks toward the praise of fruitfulness, because if anyone sows stolen wheat, a harvest is not born liable. I therefore blame the thief, but I praise the crop. I pronounce innocent him who is born from the good quality of seeds, the Apostle saying: God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body; but I condemn the shameful one who sinned from the perversity of purpose.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: One of these statements is true; the other is false.

It is true that the person born from adultery cannot excuse the guilt of the adultery, because what the adulterers did belongs to the fault of their will; what they produced, however, deserves the praise given to fertility. If someone sows stolen wheat, the harvest that grows is not guilty. So I condemn the thief but praise the crop. I pronounce the newborn innocent on account of the good quality of the seed, as the apostle says: “God gives it a body as he wishes, and to each kind of seed its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:38). But I condemn the wrongdoer, who sinned through a perverse intention.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.
